sections.s01.s0: Core pandas and plotting skills in the order you will use them on a real dataset: arrays, frames, loading, cleaning, reshaping, time series, statistics, charts. Spend about half the time on items 1 to 4, since most analysis time goes on loading and cleaning. Work every item in a notebook against one real CSV rather than toy data.
sections.s01.s1: One end-to-end analysis, from a written question to a published report. Write the question first, then the cleaning script, then the charts, then the limitations, then the report generator. Expect the cleaning script to take the largest share of the time.

s01.s0.0.how: Create arrays with np.arange and np.zeros, check .dtype and .shape, then add a (3, 1) array to a (4,) array and predict the result shape before running it. Rewrite one Python loop over a list as a single vectorised expression and time both with %timeit.
s01.s0.0.done: You can predict the shape of a broadcast result, or say why it raises, before running it.

s01.s0.1.how: Select rows and columns with loc (labels) and iloc (positions), including a boolean mask. Then write df[mask]["b"] = 1, observe that df is unchanged, and rewrite it as one call: df.loc[mask, "b"] = 1.
s01.s0.1.done: You can explain why chained assignment writes to a temporary copy and fix it with one loc call.

s01.s0.2.how: Load the same small dataset from CSV, JSON and an SQLite table with read_csv, read_json and read_sql. Pass dtype= and parse_dates= on load, then confirm with df.dtypes that no column is left as object by mistake.
s01.s0.2.done: Every column loads with the intended dtype, and dates arrive as datetime64 without a separate conversion step.

s01.s0.3.how: On a messy CSV, count missing values with isna().sum(), remove duplicates with drop_duplicates, normalise category spellings with str.strip().str.lower() and a mapping, and flag outliers with an IQR rule. Record each decision and the row count before and after.
s01.s0.3.done: You can state, for each cleaning step, how many rows it changed and why that choice was acceptable.

s01.s0.4.how: Answer three questions on one dataset: a groupby with named aggregations in agg, a pivot_table across two categories, and a merge with a lookup table. Turn the pivot back into long form with melt, and check the row count after each merge to catch duplicated keys.
s01.s0.4.done: You can pick between groupby, pivot_table and merge for a new question without looking it up.

s01.s0.5.how: Load a timestamped dataset, set a DatetimeIndex, resample it to daily and monthly totals with resample, and add a 7-day rolling mean. Attach a zone with tz_localize, convert with tz_convert, then inspect the rows around a daylight-saving change.
s01.s0.5.done: You can produce a monthly series with a rolling mean and explain what happens to the data at a DST change.

s01.s0.6.how: Run describe, plot a histogram of each numeric column, and compute corr for two pairs. For one strong correlation, name a variable that could cause both, then check whether the correlation still holds within groups of that variable.
s01.s0.6.done: You can describe a distribution's centre, spread and skew, and say why a given correlation may not be causal.

s01.s0.7.how: Compare two groups with scipy.stats.ttest_ind and with scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu, then compute a confidence interval for the difference in means with scipy.stats.bootstrap. Write each test's assumptions next to the call and check them on your data.
s01.s0.7.done: You can say in plain words what a p-value and a 95% interval mean, and when a t-test does not apply.

s01.s0.8.how: Using the fig, ax = plt.subplots() style, make one chart per question type: line for change over time, bar for comparison, histogram for distribution, scatter for relationship. Redo two of them in seaborn and label every axis with units.
s01.s0.8.done: Given a question, you can name the chart type that answers it and build it with labelled axes.

s01.s0.9.how: Take a working notebook, move its loading and cleaning code into functions in a .py module with an if __name__ == "__main__": block, and import that module back into the notebook. Run the script from a terminal to confirm it works on its own.
s01.s0.9.done: The same cleaning code runs from the command line and from the notebook, with no copy of it in either.

s01.s1.0.how: Browse a public data portal, pick a dataset under about 1 GB, and write the question in a README.md before downloading. State what result would answer it and which columns you expect to need.
s01.s1.0.done: The README states one answerable question and the expected columns, written before any analysis code.

s01.s1.1.how: Write clean.py that reads the untouched raw file, applies each cleaning step as a named function chained with DataFrame.pipe, and writes the cleaned file to a separate folder. Delete the output and rerun to check it rebuilds.
s01.s1.1.done: Running python clean.py on a fresh clone recreates the cleaned data with no manual steps.

s01.s1.2.how: Draft each chart in the notebook, then move it into a function that saves it with fig.savefig. Write the takeaway sentence first and adjust the chart until it shows that point without further explanation.
s01.s1.2.done: Three or more saved charts exist, each with a title, labelled axes and a takeaway the chart supports.

s01.s1.3.how: Write a limitations section covering who is in the sample and who is missing, how the data was collected, the share of missing values in each key column, and what the cleaning removed. Give numbers where you have them.
s01.s1.3.done: The report lists at least three concrete limitations with numbers, and says which conclusions each one weakens.

s01.s1.4.how: Write report.py that runs the cleaning, builds the charts and writes an HTML page using DataFrame.to_html for tables, or a PDF with PdfPages. Run it from a clean checkout, then publish the output.
s01.s1.4.done: One command regenerates the whole report from the raw file, and the published copy matches its output.
